data.q: Which attribute marks a function as a unit test in Rust?
data.e: The #[test] attribute tells Rust's test runner to treat the function as a test. It is part of the standard library's testing framework.

data.q: What macro is used to check that two values are equal in a test?
data.e: assert_eq!(left, right) panics if the two values are not equal, printing both values. assert_ne! checks for inequality.

data.q: How do you indicate that a test should panic with a specific message?
data.e: #[should_panic] marks a test as passing only if it panics. The optional `expected` parameter asserts the panic message contains that substring.

data.q: Where are unit tests typically located in a Rust project?
o: In a separate `tests/` directory at the crate root
Inside the same file as the code they test, under a `mod tests { #[cfg(test)] ... }` module
data.e: Unit tests live alongside the code in a `#[cfg(test)]` annotated module, usually named `tests`. Integration tests go in the `tests/` directory.

o: Runs the code only during `cargo bench`
Compiles the annotated item only when running tests (`cargo test`)
Marks the item as a benchmark function
Disables the item for release builds only
data.e: `#[cfg(test)]` ensures the module or function is only compiled and included when `cargo test` runs, keeping test code out of production binaries.

data.q: Which command runs all tests in a Cargo project?
data.e: `cargo test` compiles the crate in test mode and executes all functions annotated with #[test]. It also runs integration tests and doc tests.

data.q: How can you run a specific test by name?
data.e: `cargo test test_foo` filters tests whose names contain `test_foo`. You can also use `--` to pass arguments to the test binary, e.g., `cargo test -- --test-threads=1`.

data.q: What is the purpose of integration tests in Rust?
o: Test the public API of a crate as an external consumer would
data.e: Integration tests reside in `tests/` and only have access to the crate's public API, verifying the library works correctly from a user's perspective.

data.q: Which crate is the de-facto standard for micro-benchmarking in Rust?
data.e: The `criterion` crate provides statistically rigorous benchmarking, automatic outlier detection, and HTML reports. It works on stable Rust.

data.q: How do you define a benchmark using the `criterion` crate?
o: fn bench_foo(c: &mut Criterion) { c.bench_function("foo", |b| b.iter(|| foo())); }
data.e: Criterion uses a `criterion_group!` and `criterion_main!` macro setup. Benchmarks receive a `&mut Criterion` and use `bench_function` with a closure calling `iter`.

data.q: What does `cargo bench` do by default on stable Rust?
o: Compiles benchmarks but does not run them (benchmarks are unstable)
data.e: The built-in `#[bench]` attribute and `Bencher` are unstable and require a nightly toolchain. On stable, `cargo bench` only compiles bench targets. Use `criterion` for stable benchmarking.

data.q: Which macro asserts that an expression returns a `Result::Err` variant?
data.e: `assert_matches!(expr, Err(_))` from the standard library (since 1.68) or the `assert_matches` crate can pattern-match on `Result` variants. There is no dedicated `assert_err!` macro in std.

data.q: What is the purpose of `#[ignore]` on a test function?
o: Excludes the test from default runs; run with `cargo test -- --ignored`
Runs the test only in release mode
data.e: `#[ignore]` prevents the test from running during `cargo test`. Use `cargo test -- --ignored` to run only ignored tests, or `cargo test -- --include-ignored` to run all.

data.q: How do you run tests with multiple threads disabled (single-threaded)?
data.e: Pass `--test-threads=1` to the test binary via `cargo test -- --test-threads=1`. This is useful for tests that share global state or require deterministic ordering.

o: Generates documentation and runs examples in doc comments as tests
data.e: `cargo test --doc` (or just `cargo test` which includes doc tests by default) compiles and executes code blocks in documentation comments, ensuring examples stay correct.

data.q: Which testing approach generates random inputs to verify properties hold for a wide range of values?
data.e: Property-based testing (e.g., with the `proptest` or `quickcheck` crates) automatically generates many random inputs to check that specified invariants always hold.

data.q: How can you share common setup/teardown logic across multiple tests?
o: Using a `setup()` function called manually in each test
Implementing `Drop` on a test fixture struct and creating it in each test
data.e: Rust has no built-in test fixtures. The idiomatic pattern is a struct that implements `Drop` for teardown; instantiate it at the start of each test. The `Drop` impl runs when the test ends (even on panic).
